subject: Geriatrics
topic: Agitation in Dementia Non-Pharmacological Management and Beers Criteria
stem: An 82-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease residing in a specialized memory-care facility is evaluated for worsening restlessness and agitation occurring predominantly in the late afternoon and early evening ("sundowning"). Over the past week, she has been pacing the hallway, shouting that strangers are stealing her clothes, and refusing to enter her bedroom. She has not attempted to hit staff or residents and has not exhibited self-injurious behavior. Physical examination, vital signs, urinalysis, and metabolic panels are all normal, with no evidence of constipation, urinary retention, pain, or occult infection. The nursing facility administrator requests a prescription for scheduled oral quetiapine or risperidone to calm the patient during evening shifts. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prescribe scheduled oral haloperidol at bedtime to achieve rapid symptom suppression
options.explanation: Typical antipsychotics like haloperidol carry high risks of severe extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, falls, and increased mortality; they are not indicated for non-dangerous agitation.

options.text: Prescribe oral lorazepam as needed for agitation during the evening shift
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines are strongly cautioned in older adults (Beers criteria) because they frequently cause paradoxical disinhibition, worsening confusion, daytime sedation, and markedly increase fall and fracture risks.

options.text: Initiate scheduled oral diphenhydramine to promote evening relaxation and sleep
options.explanation: Diphenhydramine is a potent first-generation antihistamine with strong anticholinergic properties that precipitate acute delirium, urinary retention, and cognitive decline in dementia patients.

options.text: Implement non-pharmacological behavioral interventions, structured routines, and daytime light therapy
options.explanation: In dementia-related agitation and psychosis without immediate threat of physical harm to self or others, non-pharmacological environmental and behavioral modifications are strictly first-line. Interventions include: maintaining consistent daily routines, daytime natural light exposure, soothing sensory stimulation (music therapy), redirection, and addressing unmet physical needs (hunger, toileting, boredom). All second-generation and first-generation antipsychotics carry an FDA black-box warning for increased mortality (primarily from stroke and cardiovascular events) in elderly dementia patients and should never be used as chemical restraints for non-dangerous pacing or vocalization.

options.text: Apply bilateral wrist and vest physical restraints to prevent evening wandering
options.explanation: Physical restraints are ethically and clinically contraindicated for wandering; they exacerbate agitation, cause profound deconditioning, and increase asphyxiation and trauma risks.

Antipsychotics (atypical/typical) carry an FDA black-box warning for increased all-cause mortality (stroke, cardiovascular) in dementia and should only be used as a last resort for severe, dangerous agitation that threatens safety.

subject: Ethics
topic: Adolescent Confidentiality and Minor Consent for STI Management
stem: A 16-year-old high school student presents to the adolescent medicine clinic unaccompanied by an adult. She reports a 4-day history of dysuria, increased yellowish-green vaginal discharge, and intermenstrual pelvic cramping. She is sexually active with a new male partner for the past 2 months and uses barrier condoms inconsistently. Physical examination reveals mild lower abdominal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination, and purulent endocervical discharge without adnexal masses. Rapid nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) confirms Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis cervicitis. After discussing the diagnosis and recommended intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline therapy, the patient expresses intense fear that her parents will find out, stating: "If my father sees this on his insurance bill or finds out I have an infection, he will kick me out of the house." Which of the following is the most appropriate ethical and legal course of action?

options.text: Withhold antimicrobial treatment until her legal guardians provide written informed consent
options.explanation: Requiring parental consent for STI treatment is illegal under minor consent statutes and places the patient at imminent risk for pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, and tubal infertility.

options.text: Contact her parents immediately because a minor cannot legally consent to prescription medications
options.explanation: Minors are legally emancipated for the specific purposes of sexual healthcare, substance abuse counseling, and mental health emergencies in almost all jurisdictions; contacting parents violates medical ethics and state law.

options.text: Report the encounter to Child Protective Services for suspected parental medical neglect
options.explanation: There is no indication of parental abuse or neglect; the adolescent is proactively seeking healthcare independently, which does not trigger CPS reporting.

options.text: Agree to treat only if she permits the clinic social worker to notify her school guidance counselor
options.explanation: Conditioning medical treatment on disclosing sensitive reproductive health information to third parties (school officials) is a direct breach of patient confidentiality and autonomy.

options.text: Provide confidential treatment without notifying her parents and arrange billing to protect her privacy
options.explanation: In the United States, all 50 states and the District of Columbia legally permit minors to consent independently to the confidential diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), contraceptive services, and substance abuse without parental notification or consent. Breaching adolescent confidentiality damages the patient-provider relationship and discourages adolescents from seeking essential healthcare. The physician should validate her concerns, provide standard antimicrobial treatment, offer confidential partner notification services, and ensure billing and laboratory notifications do not inadvertently disclose sensitive details to the policyholder.
